title: Local Sensitivity in Exponential Selection:Failure Modes and Valid Calibrations

paper.title: Local Sensitivity in Exponential Selection: Failure Modes and Valid Calibrations
paper.abstract:
Abstract Selection is a task that chooses one element from a finite public candidate range to maximize a data-dependent score.
In differential privacy (DP), the exponential mechanism (EM) samples a candidate at a temperature calibrated to the global sensitivity.
In this paper, we study when dataset-dependent sensitivity can safely replace global sensitivity in private selection.
Naive applications of local sensitivity and smooth sensitivity fail.
Local sensitivities of two neighboring datasets can differ arbitrarily, making their output distributions differ significantly even when they have the same score vectors.
We also prove that no smooth sensitivity calibrated by any fixed smoothness and fixed temperature coefficient can guarantee range-independent ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) -DP. We propose three valid approaches.
First, a private, high-probability upper bound on local sensitivity yields approximate DP, and the method extends to finite higher-order sensitivity hierarchies.
Second, our Propose-Test-Release (PTR) variant privately searches a finite public grid for a temperature scale rather than fixing it in advance.
Third, smooth sensitivity supports several designs.
A candidate-independent smooth geometric construction produces a sensitivity envelope that is admissible under the local dampening framework, which privacy is guaranteed for any admissible envelope.
Additionally, a separate logarithmic transformation utilizes smooth sensitivity to produce a smoothed candidate score function with advantages: having controlled global sensitivity, and preserving the maximizers of the original utility score, i.e., candidates maximizing the utility.
Both of the designs yield range-independent pure DP.
Besides that, we also give two approximate DP private selectors using smooth sensitivity: a direct EM with smooth sensitivity calibrated to the candidate range and privacy parameters that matches a theoretical lower bound up to some constant factor, and one using a privatized smooth upper scale by analyzing the logarithmic transform of the smoothness.
For every proposed mechanism, we derive a high-probability regret bound under its stated conditions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Data analysis queries often fall into two types: numeric and selection. Numeric queries calculate numeric values, for example, a scalar or a vector, directly from the input dataset. Selection queries take a dataset and a set of candidate answers as input, and select one candidate to optimize some quality score function, i.e., choosing the best candidate. Differential Privacy (DP) [ 9 ] is a privacy standard (informally, together with its framework) that protects the privacy of private datasets, by guaranteeing the output distributions on every pair of neighboring datasets to be close. For numeric queries, DP is usually achieved by injecting noise, drawn from some random distributions, into the true output [ 9 ] . Noise is carefully calibrated by sensitivity, a measurement that quantifies the change in output when the input changes slightly. Global sensitivity is the worst case change, that is publicly known for each query within a universe of datasets, i.e., the set of all valid datasets. Calibrating noise via finite global sensitivity is straightforward. For standard private numeric mechanisms, all datasets receive noise from the same law and scale, with the noise magnitude being proportional to the global sensitivity of the queries [ 9 , 39 ] . Local sensitivity and its variants [ 39 , 17 ] , such as smooth sensitivity [ 34 ] , are methods to use the geometry around one specific dataset, instead of assuming the worst case as in global sensitivity. Local sensitivity is the change in the output of a query when a specific input dataset changes a little bit. While local sensitivity can change arbitrarily across nearby datasets, the smooth sensitivity is an upper bound on local sensitivity, and its values on nearby datasets are not too different from each other, where the relative change is determined by the “smoothness”. Noise is then calibrated specifically for each dataset, which allows the output to receive less noise when the private input (and its local neighborhood datasets) has low local sensitivity, improving the accuracy. The trade-off often lies in the computational cost [ 17 , 34 , 30 ] . For selection queries, given a private dataset x x , a public candidate range (set) of answers ℛ \mathcal{R} of size | ℛ | = m |\mathcal{R}|=m , a utility function q ⁡ ( x , r ) , r ∈ ℛ q(x,r),r\in\mathcal{R} indicates how good a candidate r r is as the final answer. Without privacy, it is obvious that an optimal solution is always to return the candidates that maximize the utility function, i.e., maximizers or arg ​ max r ∈ ℛ ⁡ q ​ ( x , r ) \argmax_{r\in\mathcal{R}}q(x,r) . The exponential mechanism (EM) [ 26 ] is the standard method to release a private selection. It assigns more probability mass to candidates with higher utility score, with each candidate r r ’s probability proportional partially to an exponent of ( q ⁡ ( x , r ) ) (q(x,r)) and partially to an exponent of the inverse of a term called temperature, i.e. ∝ exp ⁡ ( ( q ⁡ ( x , r ) ) temp ) \propto\exp(\frac{(q(x,r))}{\operatorname{temp}}) , hence the name "exponential". In the standard form of EM, the temperature “ temp \operatorname{temp} ” scales with the global sensitivity of q ( . , . ) q(.,.) and the inverse of privacy parameter ε \varepsilon . The regret of an answer a a , max r ⁡ q ⁡ ( x , r ) − q ⁡ ( x , a ) ≥ 0 \max_{r}q(x,r)-q(x,a)\geq 0 , measures how much utility cost we pay to output a a instead of the optimal answer. High global sensitivity yields high temperature, which spreads the probability mass among candidates, widening the regret bound, while small global sensitivity gives low temperature, which focuses the probability mass towards candidates with high utility score. While local sensitivity and its variants have been extensively applied to numeric queries for more accurate private mechanisms, they are still underutilized for selection queries. It is tempting to replace the global sensitivity in EM by these local variants, with the hope that we can tailor the output distribution for each specific dataset when it does not need the highest temperature dictated by the worst case global sensitivity. In this paper, we study the question: For finite-range private selection, how do we calibrate EM using local sensitivity and its related concepts and what are their rigorous utility bounds? The generalized EM [ 36 ] already improves selection when candidate public sensitivities are available. Our problem is different. We study a different setting: a common data-dependent calibration for all candidates, rather than per-candidate data-independent scales. We explore three main directions in search of alternatives to global sensitivity: 1. A data-dependent local sensitivity can be used for direct temperature scaling after being privatized and one-sided upper bounded on its true value (with high probability). Although a one-level local sensitivity can be fairly clean, generalizing it to higher-order hierarchies of local sensitivity, e.g., local sensitivity of local sensitivity and further derivatives [ 17 , 30 ] , can be challenging, due to the privacy and failure probability cascading across multiple levels. 2. Using Propose-Test-Release (PTR) [ 8 ] to propose a bound on local sensitivity to scale the temperature. If the proposed value is not sufficient for privacy, we might refuse to release an answer. PTR for EM has been studied, but the main challenge (and its weakness) is its dependence on a proposed value in the PTR’s simplest form, which seems difficult to estimate. 3. Extending smooth sensitivity for EM. Prior work observes that naive replacement of global sensitivity by smooth sensitivity in EM is not sufficient for privacy [ 13 , 5 ] . Therefore, the challenges of this approach include finding a flexible intermediate component that can adapt to both EM and smooth sensitivity for a unified solution, and the complexity of analyzing the regret bounds due to multiple complex components.

sections.heading: 1.1 Contributions
sections.text: Our main contributions are as follows: • We present explicit counterexamples for the direct applications of local and smooth sensitivities in setting the temperature scale in EM. We show that local sensitivity requires the additive privacy parameter δ \delta close to 1 / 2 1/2 , contrary to the principle that δ \delta is “cryptographically negligible” [ 39 , 9 ] . For smooth sensitivity, a multiplicity construction denies any fixed range-independent approximate-DP at every fixed range-independent smoothness. • We utilize the private upper bound on local sensitivity to design a conditional EM to achieve approximate DP. We then prove a recursive theorem for higher-order local sensitivity hierarchies, allowing privacy and regret bound to be propagated through all levels. • Inspired by [ 21 ] , we binary search for a safe temperature scale using a 1 1 -Lipschitz lower bound on distance to unsafe datasets under the PTR framework. It addresses the current issue of the fixed scale PTR approach for EM that relies on an arbitrary “proposed” upper bound on local sensitivity, that is unclear how to set correctly and effectively. • We give a smooth geometric envelope function that is admissible under the local dampening [ 11 ] . Distinctively, we design a logarithmic co-transformation of both utility score and smooth sensitivity, proved stable by a direct Lipschitz argument, before applying EM with transformed utility scores. Both methods achieve pure DP and preserve maximizers, i.e., candidates that maximize the utility scores. We derive explicit instance-dependent regret bounds in terms of the original utility score q ⁡ ( x , r ) q(x,r) . • We propose two alternative utilizations of smooth sensitivity. The first uses a categorical Gibbs law directly calibrated by smooth sensitivity that requires the smoothness to shrink with range size m m , and privacy parameters ( ε , δ \varepsilon,\delta ). Our smoothness matches the theoretical lower bound required for privacy up to some constants depending only on ε \varepsilon . The second route is by privatizing the smooth sensitivity. • We provide rigorous regret bounds for all methods. Furthermore, we prove two theoretical lower bounds for temperature scales required for privacy: one for unequal scales of two neighboring datasets, the other for the required smoothness of direct application of smooth sensitivity. • We apply the private upper bound on local sensitivity method, replacing the global sensitivity in EM, in solving problems to find a vertex (or an induced subgraph of size k k ) that is included in (or contains) the maximum number of copies of a motif H H [ 10 , 20 , 4 ] . In the simplest form, H H is an ℓ \ell -clique. This family of problems have applications in many domains such as biomedical [ 25 ] , document summarization [ 20 ] , and communication [ 6 ] . We show that our high-probability regret bounds on Erdős–Rényi graphs are significantly better than the worst case bounds when the graphs are sparse. sections.heading: 1.2 Structure of the paper
sections.text: We present our results in the following structure. Section 2 (Prelims) presents the privacy model, standard tools for private selection: the Exponential mechanism and the Gibbs law, different notions of sensitivity, and utility measurement. Section 3 discusses existing studies in private selection, local sensitivity and its variants in private mechanism design. Section 4 shows how straightforward applications of local sensitivity and smooth sensitivity fail to guarantee DP, and makes the claim that fixed smoothness smooth sensitivity cannot provide range-independent DP. Section 5 presents the first valid calibration of EM using privatized upper bounds on local sensitivity, that can be extended to multiple layers of local sensitivities. Section 6 describes an adaptive, private search for an upper bound on local sensitivity, utilizing efficient, tractable lower bound certificates for distances to high sensitivity datasets. Section 7 discusses several strategies to apply smooth sensitivity to calibrate EM. The first two transformation methods target the utility score, replacing the original score by new scores with bounded or controllable global sensitivity, guaranteeing range-independent pure DP. The third and fourth utilize the smoothness, either scaling it by the candidate range’s size, or using it to calibrate its logarithmic transformation for privacy, yielding weaker approximate DP. Section 8 discusses more quantitative challenges in using variants of local sensitivity, stating the dependency of the Gibbs law temperature of two neighbor datasets, and the maximum smoothness factor in terms of the range and privacy parameters to achieve DP. Finally, Section 9 demonstrates using our methods to obtain significant improvements for a family of vertex/subgraph selection problems in some regimes of input.

sections.heading: 3 Related work
sections.text: The exponential mechanism (EM) is an established standard method for private selection [ 9 , 26 , 28 , 3 ] , where the private mechanism samples from a set of public candidates, favoring ones with higher utility scores. EM has been an important building block in various differentially private algorithms [ 32 , 29 , 16 , 33 , 14 ] . [ 26 ] proposes the canonical form of EM, using a common (to all candidates) public sensitivity to calibrate the temperature of the sample distribution. [ 36 ] generalizes EM, using public per-candidate sensitivities to transform utility to have unit sensitivity before applying EM. Our work targets a divergent setting: EM calibrated by an all-candidate dataset-dependent sensitivity. Sensitivity is an important concept in differential privacy, that quantifies the change of output when the input dataset is changed slightly. Sensitivity is used to calibrate noise injection for numeric queries [ 8 , 9 , 39 ] . EM uses sensitivity to set the temperature of candidate sampling distribution [ 26 ] . Unlike global sensitivity of a function which is the worst case sensitivity across possible input datasets, local sensitivity, which is measured at a specific input dataset, is not enough for privacy protection of numeric queries by itself [ 39 , 34 ] . [ 17 ] utilizes second-order local sensitivity to construct a private upper bound on the first-order local sensitivity for some graph statistics. [ 24 ] uses a repeated shifted Laplace upper bound through higher orders. [ 30 ] further generalizes the concept to higher-order sensitivity hierarchies for private subgraph counting. The Propose-Test-Release (PTR) framework [ 8 ] uses local sensitivity in a different way: it proposes a sensitivity bound, either publicly known or privately released (Propose phase), it calculates the (noisy) distance from the input dataset to the region of datasets whose local sensitivity is not bounded by the proposed value and checks if the distance is safe (Test phase) for privacy before finally injecting noise calibrated by the public bound or abstaining from answering (Release phase). [ 34 ] proposes the smooth sensitivity framework, which is a smooth upper bound on local sensitivity, in which their values at two neighboring datasets do not differ multiplicatively by more than a smoothness value ( e β ) (\mathrm{e}^{\beta}) . Using the smooth sensitivity to calibrate a one-dimensional Cauchy noise gives pure DP, and a Laplacian noise yields approximate DP. [ 41 ] constructs ladder functions that produce quality scores with unit global sensitivity ( G ​ S = 1 GS=1 ) from sensitivity at increasing distance from the input dataset. [ 11 ] shares similar ideas with the ladder function, defines an admissible sensitivity function indexed by radius, uses it to transform the utility score to have unit global sensitivity and applies the traditional EM to the transformed scores. In this paper, we adapt this framework, using smooth sensitivity to construct admissible envelopes and derive their rigorous regret bounds. Most local variants of sensitivity and their related quantities have been initially proposed for numeric queries. There are few attempts at adapting them for EM [ 27 , 2 , 38 , 7 ] . EM has been incorporated into the PTR framework [ 23 , 37 , 35 ] . The fixed scale PTR [ 23 , 35 ] relies on a known public bound b + b^{+} on local sensitivity, and the calculation of the distance to high sensitivity datasets, which raise some practical issues that we will discuss further in Appendix B . For numeric queries, [ 21 ] proposes a noisy binary search over b + ∈ { 1 , … , ⌈ G ​ S f ⌉ } b^{+}\in\{1,\ldots,\lceil GS_{f}\rceil\} , assuming a finite public global sensitivity G ​ S f GS_{f} or its upper bound, and replaces each threshold’s possibly intractable exact distance to high sensitivity datasets by a threshold-dependent nonnegative, 1-Lipschitz lower certificate. The 2021 addendum [ 12 ] to [ 13 ] acknowledges that its direct smooth sensitivity substitution lacks a formal privacy proof and reports an observation that the privacy may not always be guaranteed. Subsequently, [ 5 ] formally forms a counterexample, claiming such substitution does not necessarily meet the pure DP standard. Their claim fixes the temperature coefficient and the smoothness to the target privacy parameter as λ = ε / 2 = 0.25 \lambda=\varepsilon/2=0.25 and β = ε = 0.5 \beta=\varepsilon=0.5 . Both results do not establish an impossibility uniformly over independently fixed smoothness and temperature coefficient. Smooth sensitivity has been used in private selection , though the following work does not directly use it to set the temperature of the categorical Gibbs law (Eq. ( 1 )). [ 22 ] studies a more general formulation of private selection, in which each candidate is a DP mechanism, with noise calibrated by smooth sensitivity as one possible instantiation. The framework utilizes an oracle model, using a random number of oracle calls, instead of sampling from the categorical Gibbs law. It can improve the utility bound when a utility-maximizing candidate has low smooth sensitivity. [ 28 ] studies the selection problem using a related continuous Gibbs-posterior under Euclidean, convex/Lipschitz-loss, and strongly log-concave-prior conditions, not the finite-candidate selection problem. [ 1 ] addresses the problem along a different axis, using public candidate-specific global sensitivities instead of our dataset-specific sensitivity approach. It also shows that naive independent score perturbation calibrated separately to these sensitivities need not satisfy DP. There is a family of approaches called perturb-and-select [ 9 ] , that first privatizes the utility score and selects the candidates, either by argmax or sampling. Cauchy noise generated by smooth sensitivity can be applied directly to the vector of utility scores of all candidates [ 34 ] , followed by an argmax or Gibbs sample from the noisy vector which serves as post-processing with no extra incurred privacy cost. In order for noise to be added to each coordinate, it requires a norm-specific local sensitivity analysis and the calibration depends on candidate range. [ 40 ] recently uses smooth sensitivity, but also with range-dependent calibration to privatize the utility scores. [ 15 ] improves the smooth noise for single real-valued queries. [ 5 ] proposes smooth noisy max, utilizing a common smooth upper bound on local sensitivity, admitting some families of noise, demonstrating its effectiveness over global sensitivity on various tasks: percentile selection, decision tree, and random forest.

sections.heading: 7 Smooth Sensitivity
sections.text: In previous sections, we replace the public scale b b by privacy-protected functions, hoping that their values are not as large as the public value GS q \operatorname{GS}_{q} while keeping the original utility score q ⁡ ( x , r ) q(x,r) . In this section, we explore a different variant of local sensitivity, namely the smooth sensitivity. The smooth sensitivity is an upper bound on local sensitivity at every dataset x x , together with a constraint of its smoothness: the ratio of its values on x ∼ x ′ x\sim x^{\prime} is upper bounded by e β e^{\beta} . Section 4 confirms that straightforward application of smooth sensitivity does not provide a privacy guarantee. In this section, we explore several different approaches. The first and second methods (Section 7.1 and Section 7.2 ) utilize smooth sensitivity to transform the original utility score to ones with bounded or controllable global sensitivity. The third and fourth methods (Section 7.3 ) utilize the smoothness factor, but in different ways: scaling the smoothness by privacy and range statistics, or privatizing its logarithmic function by the smoothness. The first two methods show some advantages, by providing range-independent pure DP while retaining the maximizing candidates. The first method is based on the local dampening framework. Appendix C presents the rigorous analysis and further discussions of the adapted framework. The dampening framework provides the privacy template but still requires an admissible envelope and a utility translation, which we use a geometric transformation of the smooth sensitivity to design. The separate, independent method combines smooth sensitivity and the original utility score in the form of a logarithmic transformation to generate a new score. The global sensitivity of the new score can be parameterized by changing some constant factors of the transformation, allowing us to achieve a desired public regret bound.

sections.heading: 10 Conclusions
sections.text: We study the general problem of using local information for private selection, aiming to replace the public worst case global sensitivity in the exponential selection by local variants of sensitivity. We prove that straightforward, direct replacements using local and smooth sensitivity with fixed smoothness do not guarantee privacy, even under the approximate DP. Instead, we show that privacy of exponential selection can be achieved by several careful adaptations of local sensitivity, in particular, a privatized one-sided high probability upper bound on local sensitivity, the adaptive PTR framework, and the co-transformation of the smooth sensitivity and utility score, among others. We also provide their regret bounds, which are instance-specific and utilize local geometric properties of the private input datasets. Applying our technique to some vertex/subgraph selection problems shows significant improvements over the global sensitivity for a family of Erdős–Rényi graphs with reasonable edge density assumptions. Correspondence to: dungtien.nguyen@utsa.edu Anil Vullikanti † † thanks: University of Virginia Abstract Selection is a task that chooses one element from a finite public candidate range to maximize a data-dependent score. In differential privacy (DP), the exponential mechanism (EM) samples a candidate at a temperature calibrated to the global sensitivity. In this paper, we study when dataset-dependent sensitivity can safely replace global sensitivity in private selection. Naive applications of local sensitivity and smooth sensitivity fail. Local sensitivities of two neighboring datasets can differ arbitrarily, making their output distributions differ significantly even when they have the same score vectors. We also prove that no smooth sensitivity calibrated by any fixed smoothness and fixed temperature coefficient can guarantee range-independent ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) -DP. We propose three valid approaches. First, a private, high-probability upper bound on local sensitivity yields approximate DP, and the method extends to finite higher-order sensitivity hierarchies. Second, our Propose-Test-Release (PTR) variant privately searches a finite public grid for a temperature scale rather than fixing it in advance. Third, smooth sensitivity supports several designs. A candidate-independent smooth geometric construction produces a sensitivity envelope that is admissible under the local dampening framework, which privacy is guaranteed for any admissible envelope. Additionally, a separate logarithmic transformation utilizes smooth sensitivity to produce a smoothed candidate score function with advantages: having controlled global sensitivity, and preserving the maximizers of the original utility score, i.e., candidates maximizing the utility. Both of the designs yield range-independent pure DP. Besides that, we also give two approximate DP private selectors using smooth sensitivity: a direct EM with smooth sensitivity calibrated to the candidate range and privacy parameters that matches a theoretical lower bound up to some constant factor, and one using a privatized smooth upper scale by analyzing the logarithmic transform of the smoothness. For every proposed mechanism, we derive a high-probability regret bound under its stated conditions. 1 Introduction Data analysis queries often fall into two types: numeric and selection. Numeric queries calculate numeric values, for example, a scalar or a vector, directly from the input dataset. Selection queries take a dataset and a set of candidate answers as input, and select one candidate to optimize some quality score function, i.e., choosing the best candidate. Differential Privacy (DP) [ 9 ] is a privacy standard (informally, together with its framework) that protects the privacy of private datasets, by guaranteeing the output distributions on every pair of neighboring datasets to be close. For numeric queries, DP is usually achieved by injecting noise, drawn from some random distributions, into the true output [ 9 ] . Noise is carefully calibrated by sensitivity, a measurement that quantifies the change in output when the input changes slightly. Global sensitivity is the worst case change, that is publicly known for each query within a universe of datasets, i.e., the set of all valid datasets. Calibrating noise via finite global sensitivity is straightforward. For standard private numeric mechanisms, all datasets receive noise from the same law and scale, with the noise magnitude being proportional to the global sensitivity of the queries [ 9 , 39 ] . Local sensitivity and its variants [ 39 , 17 ] , such as smooth sensitivity [ 34 ] , are methods to use the geometry around one specific dataset, instead of assuming the worst case as in global sensitivity. Local sensitivity is the change in the output of a query when a specific input dataset changes a little bit. While local sensitivity can change arbitrarily across nearby datasets, the smooth sensitivity is an upper bound on local sensitivity, and its values on nearby datasets are not too different from each other, where the relative change is determined by the “smoothness”. Noise is then calibrated specifically for each dataset, which allows the output to receive less noise when the private input (and its local neighborhood datasets) has low local sensitivity, improving the accuracy. The trade-off often lies in the computational cost [ 17 , 34 , 30 ] . For selection queries, given a private dataset x x , a public candidate range (set) of answers ℛ \mathcal{R} of size | ℛ | = m |\mathcal{R}|=m , a utility function q ⁡ ( x , r ) , r ∈ ℛ q(x,r),r\in\mathcal{R} indicates how good a candidate r r is as the final answer. Without privacy, it is obvious that an optimal solution is always to return the candidates that maximize the utility function, i.e., maximizers or arg ​ max r ∈ ℛ ⁡ q ​ ( x , r ) \argmax_{r\in\mathcal{R}}q(x,r) . The exponential mechanism (EM) [ 26 ] is the standard method to release a private selection. It assigns more probability mass to candidates with higher utility score, with each candidate r r ’s probability proportional partially to an exponent of ( q ⁡ ( x , r ) ) (q(x,r)) and partially to an exponent of the inverse of a term called temperature, i.e. ∝ exp ⁡ ( ( q ⁡ ( x , r ) ) temp ) \propto\exp(\frac{(q(x,r))}{\operatorname{temp}}) , hence the name "exponential". In the standard form of EM, the temperature “ temp \operatorname{temp} ” scales with the global sensitivity of q ( . , . ) q(.,.) and the inverse of privacy parameter ε \varepsilon . The regret of an answer a a , max r ⁡ q ⁡ ( x , r ) − q ⁡ ( x , a ) ≥ 0 \max_{r}q(x,r)-q(x,a)\geq 0 , measures how much utility cost we pay to output a a instead of the optimal answer. High global sensitivity yields high temperature, which spreads the probability mass among candidates, widening the regret bound, while small global sensitivity gives low temperature, which focuses the probability mass towards candidates with high utility score. While local sensitivity and its variants have been extensively applied to numeric queries for more accurate private mechanisms, they are still underutilized for selection queries. It is tempting to replace the global sensitivity in EM by these local variants, with the hope that we can tailor the output distribution for each specific dataset when it does not need the highest temperature dictated by the worst case global sensitivity. In this paper, we study the question: For finite-range private selection, how do we calibrate EM using local sensitivity and its related concepts and what are their rigorous utility bounds? The generalized EM [ 36 ] already improves selection when candidate public sensitivities are available. Our problem is different. We study a different setting: a common data-dependent calibration for all candidates, rather than per-candidate data-independent scales. We explore three main directions in search of alternatives to global sensitivity: 1. A data-dependent local sensitivity can be used for direct temperature scaling after being privatized and one-sided upper bounded on its true value (with high probability). Although a one-level local sensitivity can be fairly clean, generalizing it to higher-order hierarchies of local sensitivity, e.g., local sensitivity of local sensitivity and further derivatives [ 17 , 30 ] , can be challenging, due to the privacy and failure probability cascading across multiple levels. 2. Using Propose-Test-Release (PTR) [ 8 ] to propose a bound on local sensitivity to scale the temperature. If the proposed value is not sufficient for privacy, we might refuse to release an answer. PTR for EM has been studied, but the main challenge (and its weakness) is its dependence on a proposed value in the PTR’s simplest form, which seems difficult to estimate. 3. Extending smooth sensitivity for EM. Prior work observes that naive replacement of global sensitivity by smooth sensitivity in EM is not sufficient for privacy [ 13 , 5 ] . Therefore, the challenges of this approach include finding a flexible intermediate component that can adapt to both EM and smooth sensitivity for a unified solution, and the complexity of analyzing the regret bounds due to multiple complex components. 1.1 Contributions Our main contributions are as follows: • We present explicit counterexamples for the direct applications of local and smooth sensitivities in setting the temperature scale in EM. We show that local sensitivity requires the additive privacy parameter δ \delta close to 1 / 2 1/2 , contrary to the principle that δ \delta is “cryptographically negligible” [ 39 , 9 ] . For smooth sensitivity, a multiplicity construction denies any fixed range-independent approximate-DP at every fixed range-independent smoothness. • We utilize the private upper bound on local sensitivity to design a conditional EM to achieve approximate DP. We then prove a recursive theorem for higher-order local sensitivity hierarchies, allowing privacy and regret bound to be propagated through all levels. • Inspired by [ 21 ] , we binary search for a safe temperature scale using a 1 1 -Lipschitz lower bound on distance to unsafe datasets under the PTR framework. It addresses the current issue of the fixed scale PTR approach for EM that relies on an arbitrary “proposed” upper bound on local sensitivity, that is unclear how to set correctly and effectively. • We give a smooth geometric envelope function that is admissible under the local dampening [ 11 ] . Distinctively, we design a logarithmic co-transformation of both utility score and smooth sensitivity, proved stable by a direct Lipschitz argument, before applying EM with transformed utility scores. Both methods achieve pure DP and preserve maximizers, i.e., candidates that maximize the utility scores. We derive explicit instance-dependent regret bounds in terms of the original utility score q ⁡ ( x , r ) q(x,r) . • We propose two alternative utilizations of smooth sensitivity. The first uses a categorical Gibbs law directly calibrated by smooth sensitivity that requires the smoothness to shrink with range size m m , and privacy parameters ( ε , δ \varepsilon,\delta ). Our smoothness matches the theoretical lower bound required for privacy up to some constants depending only on ε \varepsilon . The second route is by privatizing the smooth sensitivity. • We provide rigorous regret bounds for all methods. Furthermore, we prove two theoretical lower bounds for temperature scales required for privacy: one for unequal scales of two neighboring datasets, the other for the required smoothness of direct application of smooth sensitivity. • We apply the private upper bound on local sensitivity method, replacing the global sensitivity in EM, in solving problems to find a vertex (or an induced subgraph of size k k ) that is included in (or contains) the maximum number of copies of a motif H H [ 10 , 20 , 4 ] . In the simplest form, H H is an ℓ \ell -clique. This family of problems have applications in many domains such as biomedical [ 25 ] , document summarization [ 20 ] , and communication [ 6 ] . We show that our high-probability regret bounds on Erdős–Rényi graphs are significantly better than the worst case bounds when the graphs are sparse. Section 2 (Prelims) presents the privacy model, standard tools for private selection: the Exponential mechanism and the Gibbs law, different notions of sensitivity, and utility measurement. Section 3 discusses existing studies in private selection, local sensitivity and its variants in private mechanism design. Section 4 shows how straightforward applications of local sensitivity and smooth sensitivity fail to guarantee DP, and makes the claim that fixed smoothness smooth sensitivity cannot provide range-independent DP. Section 5 presents the first valid calibration of EM using privatized upper bounds on local sensitivity, that can be extended to multiple layers of local sensitivities. Section 6 describes an adaptive, private search for an upper bound on local sensitivity, utilizing efficient, tractable lower bound certificates for distances to high sensitivity datasets. Section 7 discusses several strategies to apply smooth sensitivity to calibrate EM. The first two transformation methods target the utility score, replacing the original score by new scores with bounded or controllable global sensitivity, guaranteeing range-independent pure DP. The third and fourth utilize the smoothness, either scaling it by the candidate range’s size, or using it to calibrate its logarithmic transformation for privacy, yielding weaker approximate DP. Section 8 discusses more quantitative challenges in using variants of local sensitivity, stating the dependency of the Gibbs law temperature of two neighbor datasets, and the maximum smoothness factor in terms of the range and privacy parameters to achieve DP. EM has been an important building block in various differentially private algorithms [ 32 , 29 , 16 , 33 , 14 ] . [ 26 ] proposes the canonical form of EM, using a common (to all candidates) public sensitivity to calibrate the temperature of the sample distribution. [ 36 ] generalizes EM, using public per-candidate sensitivities to transform utility to have unit sensitivity before applying EM. Our work targets a divergent setting: EM calibrated by an all-candidate dataset-dependent sensitivity. Sensitivity is an important concept in differential privacy, that quantifies the change of output when the input dataset is changed slightly. Sensitivity is used to calibrate noise injection for numeric queries [ 8 , 9 , 39 ] . EM uses sensitivity to set the temperature of candidate sampling distribution [ 26 ] . Unlike global sensitivity of a function which is the worst case sensitivity across possible input datasets, local sensitivity, which is measured at a specific input dataset, is not enough for privacy protection of numeric queries by itself [ 39 , 34 ] . [ 17 ] utilizes second-order local sensitivity to construct a private upper bound on the first-order local sensitivity for some graph statistics. [ 24 ] uses a repeated shifted Laplace upper bound through higher orders. [ 30 ] further generalizes the concept to higher-order sensitivity hierarchies for private subgraph counting. The Propose-Test-Release (PTR) framework [ 8 ] uses local sensitivity in a different way: it proposes a sensitivity bound, either publicly known or privately released (Propose phase), it calculates the (noisy) distance from the input dataset to the region of datasets whose local sensitivity is not bounded by the proposed value and checks if the distance is safe (Test phase) for privacy before finally injecting noise calibrated by the public bound or abstaining from answering (Release phase). [ 34 ] proposes the smooth sensitivity framework, which is a smooth upper bound on local sensitivity, in which their values at two neighboring datasets do not differ multiplicatively by more than a smoothness value ( e β ) (\mathrm{e}^{\beta}) . Using the smooth sensitivity to calibrate a one-dimensional Cauchy noise gives pure DP, and a Laplacian noise yields approximate DP. [ 41 ] constructs ladder functions that produce quality scores with unit global sensitivity ( G ​ S = 1 GS=1 ) from sensitivity at increasing distance from the input dataset. [ 11 ] shares similar ideas with the ladder function, defines an admissible sensitivity function indexed by radius, uses it to transform the utility score to have unit global sensitivity and applies the traditional EM to the transformed scores. In this paper, we adapt this framework, using smooth sensitivity to construct admissible envelopes and derive their rigorous regret bounds. Most local variants of sensitivity and their related quantities have been initially proposed for numeric queries. There are few attempts at adapting them for EM [ 27 , 2 , 38 , 7 ] . EM has been incorporated into the PTR framework [ 23 , 37 , 35 ] . The fixed scale PTR [ 23 , 35 ] relies on a known public bound b + b^{+} on local sensitivity, and the calculation of the distance to high sensitivity datasets, which raise some practical issues that we will discuss further in Appendix B .
